candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — dosage adjustment, anticoagulant monitoring and adverse-effect prevention
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — argatroban in hepatic impairment
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize hepatic impairment as a major argatroban dosing and monitoring consideration in HIT.

options.A: Question the order because hepatic impairment substantially reduces argatroban clearance and current labeling recommends a lower initial dose with close aPTT-guided titration
options.B: Administer the usual initial infusion because argatroban is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and hepatic impairment does not affect exposure
options.C: Replace argatroban with unfractionated heparin because heparin is preferred when HIT has already been diagnosed
options.D: Administer argatroban without coagulation monitoring because direct thrombin inhibitors do not require laboratory titration in HIT

candidate.rationale: Argatroban is an approved nonheparin anticoagulant for adult HIT. In moderate or severe hepatic impairment, clearance is markedly reduced and current labeling recommends a lower initial infusion with careful aPTT monitoring and titration. For HIT, aPTT is used to monitor therapy. Heparin should not be restarted simply because hepatic impairment is present.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Argatroban is indicated for adult HIT; hepatic impairment requires lower starting dose and careful aPTT titration.
candidate.source_locator: Sections 1.1, 2.2, 2.4 and 8.6 — HIT indication; aPTT monitoring; reduced initial dose in moderate/severe hepatic impairment due to decreased clearance
candidate.stem: An adult client with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and moderate hepatic impairment has an order to start argatroban at the usual initial infusion rate used for HIT in clients without hepatic impairment. Which action should the nurse take?
